# Interventions and optimization

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Workshop programme**: taught live on Day 3, Session 1. See the [full schedule](../workshop.qmd).
:::

An intervention model has two layers. First, a **scenario** specifies a
policy and simulates its consequences. Second, an **optimization** compares
many admissible policies using an explicit objective and constraints. Keeping
those layers separate makes it possible to audit a proposed policy before
asking an optimizer to choose one.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## How this chapter is used in the workshop

This session is a guided tour of what specialised packages let you do once a
model exists, rather than a complete treatment of optimisation. The scenario
half uses machinery you already have: the callback is the one that produced the
lockdown in @sec-ordinary-differential-equations, and a vaccination campaign is
the same pattern applied to a different parameter. The optimisation half
introduces one small, fully worked problem so that the *shape* of an
optimisation (decision variable, objective, bounds) becomes recognisable. The
pointers at the end of the chapter are where to go when you need more than that.
:::

## Learning goals

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- represent a temporary reduction in transmission with an ODE callback;
- distinguish a callback-driven scenario from an optimization problem;
- formulate a small bounded intervention-timing problem with
  [Optimization.jl](https://docs.sciml.ai/Optimization/stable/);
- compare an optimized policy with no intervention and a fixed reference
  policy; and
- state the objective, bounds, and limitations that determine what an
  “optimal” intervention means.

## Model assumptions and classification

The model is deterministic, continuous in time, continuous in state, and
population based. It retains the closed, homogeneous SIR assumptions of
@kermack1927 and adds a temporary intervention that reduces transmission by a
fraction $v(t)$. This is a scenario model, not an individual-level simulation:
the callback changes one population-level coefficient at specified times.

The baseline is $S(0)=990$, $I(0)=10$, $R(0)=0$, $N=1000$,
$\beta=0.05$, $c=10$, and $\gamma=0.25$. The intervention used below reduces
transmission by $v_{\max}=0.5$ for a fixed duration of 10 time units. The
decision variable is only the start time $t_1$, bounded to $0\leq t_1\leq25$.
More general time-varying controls belong in the advanced
[InfiniteOpt/SDDP unit](../appendices/08-advanced-optimal-control.html).

## Equations

We add cumulative incidence $C(t)$ as a bookkeeping state. During a policy
window, transmission is multiplied by $1-v(t)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm dS}{\mathrm dt}
  &= -\beta c(1-v(t))\frac{SI}{N},\\
\frac{\mathrm dI}{\mathrm dt}
  &= \beta c(1-v(t))\frac{SI}{N}-\gamma I,\\
\frac{\mathrm dR}{\mathrm dt}
  &= \gamma I,\\
\frac{\mathrm dC}{\mathrm dt}
  &= \beta c(1-v(t))\frac{SI}{N}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-intervention-sir}

For a rectangular policy,

$$
v(t;t_1)=
\begin{cases}
v_{\max},&t_1\leq t<t_1+d,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-rectangular-policy}

The objective in this chapter is the final cumulative incidence
$J(t_1)=C(T;t_1)$ at $T=45$. Because the intervention level and duration are
fixed, minimizing $J$ is a one-dimensional bounded problem. If intervention
cost, equity, hospital capacity, or uncertainty matters, those terms must be
added explicitly rather than inferred from this objective.

Two properties of this objective are easy to misread. First, "final" means *at
the finite decision horizon* $T=45$, not at epidemic extinction. A policy can
lower $C(45)$ partly by pushing infections past the horizon rather than by
preventing them, so both the optimal start time and the ranking of policies can
depend on $T$. If eventual epidemic size is what you care about, choose $T$
large enough that $I(T)$ is negligible and check that the answer is stable as
$T$ grows. Second, integrating $\mathrm dC/\mathrm dt$ from $C(0)=0$ gives
$C(T)=S(0)-S(T)$, so $C$ counts infections generated after time zero and
excludes the ten people who are already infectious at the start.

## Julia implementation

The right-hand side makes the policy multiplier visible. `PresetTimeCallback`
is the appropriate tool for this rectangular scenario; its official
documentation is in [DiffEqCallbacks.jl](https://docs.sciml.ai/DiffEqCallbacks/stable/).

As in the previous chapter, parameters are a plain vector rather than the named
tuple of @sec-julia-essentials, and for the same kind of reason: the callback
mutates one entry in place (`integrator.p[4]`), which a `NamedTuple` cannot do.
The comment beside each entry is doing the work the field name usually does, so
read the order carefully.

```{julia}
using CairoMakie
using DiffEqCallbacks
using EpiModelingCourse
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using Optimization
using OptimizationOptimJL

baseline = BASELINE_PARAMETERS
u0 = Float64[
    BASELINE_INITIAL_STATE.S,
    BASELINE_INITIAL_STATE.I,
    BASELINE_INITIAL_STATE.R,
    0.0,
]
time_grid = collect(0.0:0.5:45.0)
intervention_duration = 10.0
maximum_reduction = 0.5

function policy_sir!(du, u, p, t)
    β, c, γ, reduction, N = p
    S, I, R, C = u
    incidence = β * c * (1 - reduction) * S * I / N
    du[1] = -incidence
    du[2] = incidence - γ * I
    du[3] = γ * I
    du[4] = incidence
    return nothing
end
```

### Scenario simulation with a callback

`run_scenario` sets the fourth parameter at $t_1$ and restores it at $t_1+d$.
The callback does not optimize anything; it implements one policy that
has already been specified.

That fourth parameter is initialized to the value the policy takes at $t=0$
rather than to zero. For every $t_1>0$ the two are the same, but at the lower
bound $t_1=0$ the callback event coincides with the initial time, and whether
such an event fires before the first step is a detail of the callback
implementation rather than something @eq-rectangular-policy says. Setting the
initial value explicitly makes the admissible policy $t_1=0$ implement the
equation regardless, so the objective is continuous at the edge of the box.

The test is `start_time <= 0.0 < stop_time` and not merely `start_time <= 0.0`,
because it has to answer "is the policy window open at $t=0$?" rather than "does
it start at $t=0$?". Those differ in exactly one case: a zero-duration policy at
$t_1=0$, whose window $[0,0)$ is empty and which must therefore mean *no
intervention*. That case is not hypothetical — Exercise 2 makes the duration a
decision variable, and $d=0$ is the policy the optimizer selects once the cost
weight is large enough. Passing the same times through `unique` keeps the
degenerate case from registering one instant twice.

```{julia}
function run_scenario(
    start_time;
    duration = intervention_duration,
    reduction = maximum_reduction,
    horizon = last(time_grid),
)
    stop_time = start_time + duration
    initial_reduction = start_time <= 0.0 < stop_time ? reduction : 0.0
    parameters = [
        baseline.beta,           # 1: β, transmission probability per contact
        baseline.contact_rate,   # 2: c, contacts per person per unit time
        baseline.gamma,          # 3: γ, recovery rate
        initial_reduction,       # 4: v, the entry the callback mutates
        baseline.N,              # 5: N, population size
    ]
    function affect!(integrator)
        integrator.p[4] = integrator.t < stop_time ? reduction : 0.0
        return nothing
    end
    callback = PresetTimeCallback(unique([start_time, stop_time]), affect!)
    problem = ODEProblem(policy_sir!, u0, (0.0, horizon), parameters)
    return solve(
        problem,
        Tsit5();
        callback = callback,
        saveat = 0.0:0.5:horizon,
        abstol = 1e-8,
        reltol = 1e-8,
    )
end

no_intervention = solve(
    ODEProblem(
        policy_sir!,
        u0,
        (0.0, last(time_grid)),
        [baseline.beta, baseline.contact_rate, baseline.gamma, 0.0, baseline.N],
    ),
    Tsit5();
    saveat = time_grid,
    abstol = 1e-8,
    reltol = 1e-8,
)
reference_start = 8.0
reference_solution = run_scenario(reference_start)
```

The figure compares the infectious trajectories and cumulative incidence for
the no-intervention and reference scenarios.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ch11-scenarios
#| fig-cap: "A callback-defined intervention scenario compared with no intervention."
baseline_array = Array(no_intervention)
reference_array = Array(reference_solution(time_grid))
fig = Figure(size = (900, 700))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "time", ylabel = "infectious people")
lines!(ax1, time_grid, baseline_array[2, :], label = "none", color = :firebrick)
lines!(ax1, time_grid, reference_array[2, :], label = "50% reduction", color = :steelblue)
vspan!(ax1, reference_start, reference_start + intervention_duration,
    color = (:steelblue, 0.15))
axislegend(ax1, position = :rb)
ax2 = Axis(fig[2, 1], xlabel = "time", ylabel = "cumulative incidence")
lines!(ax2, time_grid, baseline_array[4, :], label = "none", color = :firebrick)
lines!(ax2, time_grid, reference_array[4, :], label = "50% reduction", color = :steelblue)
vspan!(ax2, reference_start, reference_start + intervention_duration,
    color = (:steelblue, 0.15))
fig
```

### A bounded Optimization.jl problem

Now the scenario function becomes the objective, and every optimisation problem
in the SciML stack is assembled from the same four pieces. Reading the block
below in order:

| Piece | Here | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| objective | `final_incidence(x, _)` | a function of the decision variable `x` and (unused) parameters, returning one number to minimise |
| derivative | `AutoFiniteDiff()` | how the optimiser gets slopes: a robust black-box approximation |
| starting point and box | `[reference_start]`, `lb`, `ub` | where the search begins and the range it may not leave |
| method | `Fminbox(LBFGS())` | the algorithm; `Fminbox` is the wrapper that enforces the box |

Containing an ODE solve is *not* by itself a reason to fall back on finite
differences — SciML can differentiate through many solves, and the
[universal differential equations](../appendices/04-universal-differential-equations.html)
appendix does exactly that. Finite differences are the right choice here for
narrower reasons: the callback *times* depend on the
decision variable, which makes the objective a black box to a differentiation
backend, and there is only one variable, so the cost of a numerical slope is two
extra solves. The [Optimization.jl differentiation
docs](https://docs.sciml.ai/Optimization/stable/API/ad/) list the alternatives
and their trade-offs.

`solve` is the same verb as for an `ODEProblem`: a different problem type
selects a different method. The optimizer only chooses $t_1$; it does not decide
whether the intervention is ethical, feasible to deliver, or appropriate for the
model.

```{julia}
function final_incidence(x, _)
    solution = run_scenario(x[1])
    return Array(solution)[4, end]
end

objective = OptimizationFunction(final_incidence, AutoFiniteDiff())
optimization_problem = OptimizationProblem(
    objective,
    [reference_start],
    nothing;
    lb = [0.0],
    ub = [25.0],
)
optimization_solution = solve(
    optimization_problem,
    Fminbox(LBFGS());
    maxiters = 30,
)
optimal_start = optimization_solution.u[1]
optimal_solution = run_scenario(optimal_start)
```

`Fminbox(LBFGS())` is a gradient-based *local* method: it returns a point where
the objective stops decreasing inside the box, not a certificate that no better
point exists. With one decision variable we can afford to check. The grid below
is that check — a diagnostic that gives evidence the returned local minimizer is
the relevant minimum over the declared box, not a replacement for the
optimization API.

```{julia}
candidate_starts = collect(0.0:1.0:25.0)
candidate_objectives = [final_incidence([start], nothing) for start in candidate_starts]
objective_at_optimum = final_incidence([optimal_start], nothing)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ch11-optimization
#| fig-cap: "Final cumulative incidence as intervention start time varies."
fig = Figure(size = (900, 450))
ax = Axis(
    fig[1, 1],
    xlabel = "intervention start time",
    ylabel = "final cumulative incidence",
    title = "Bounded timing optimization",
)
lines!(ax, candidate_starts, candidate_objectives, color = :darkorange)
scatter!(ax, [optimal_start], [objective_at_optimum],
    color = :firebrick, markersize = 14, label = "optimizer")
axislegend(ax)
fig
```

## Validation

The state equations imply $S+I+R=N$ and $C$ is nondecreasing. The scenario
callback should also reduce final incidence relative to no intervention for this
parameter choice, *including* at the lower bound $t_1=0$ — that is the check
that the policy is active when the callback event sits at the initial
time. Finally, the optimizer must report success, land inside the declared box,
and agree with the grid in **both** coordinates: comparing objective values
alone would pass even if the optimizer had stopped somewhere else on a flat
stretch of the curve.

```{julia}
optimal_array = Array(optimal_solution(time_grid))
conservation_error = maximum(abs.(vec(sum(optimal_array[1:3, :]; dims = 1)) .- baseline.N))
incidence_is_monotone = all(diff(optimal_array[4, :]) .>= -1e-10)
grid_minimum, grid_best_index = findmin(candidate_objectives)
grid_best_start = candidate_starts[grid_best_index]
immediate_policy_incidence = final_incidence([0.0], nothing)
empty_policy_incidence = Array(run_scenario(0.0; duration = 0.0))[4, end]

@assert conservation_error < 1e-6
@assert incidence_is_monotone
@assert 0.0 <= optimal_start <= 25.0
@assert successful_retcode(optimization_solution)
@assert abs(optimal_start - grid_best_start) <= 1.0
@assert abs(objective_at_optimum - grid_minimum) <= 1.0
@assert optimal_array[4, end] < baseline_array[4, end]
@assert immediate_policy_incidence < baseline_array[4, end]
@assert empty_policy_incidence ≈ baseline_array[4, end]
(conservation_error = conservation_error, optimal_start = optimal_start,
    grid_best_start = grid_best_start,
    final_incidence_without_policy = baseline_array[4, end],
    final_incidence_with_policy = optimal_array[4, end],
    final_incidence_starting_immediately = immediate_policy_incidence)
```

The last three assertions bracket the two degenerate corners of the box. The
optimized policy beats doing nothing, and so does the earliest admissible
policy, which is what would fail if $t_1=0$ silently meant "no intervention".
The zero-duration policy at $t_1=0$ has to fail in precisely the opposite
direction: an empty window must reproduce the no-intervention trajectory
exactly, not a permanent intervention.

One check remains, and it is the one most easily skipped: whether the answer is
an artefact of the horizon. Rerunning the same grid with $T$ extended well past
extinction is cheap, and the `horizon` keyword is there for it.

```{julia}
horizon_check = map((45.0, 90.0, 200.0)) do horizon
    objectives = [
        Array(run_scenario(start; horizon = horizon))[4, end]
        for start in candidate_starts
    ]
    index = argmin(objectives)
    return (horizon = horizon, best_start = candidate_starts[index],
        best_incidence = objectives[index],
        without_policy = Array(run_scenario(2 * horizon; horizon = horizon))[4, end])
end
```

The best start time moves later as the horizon grows, and the incidence it
achieves rises, while the no-policy column barely changes after the epidemic has
burned out. Both effects are the deferral warned about above: at $T=45$ some of
the credit an early-ish policy receives is for infections that had merely been
postponed, and lengthening the horizon takes that credit back. The
$T=90$ and $T=200$ rows agree with each other, which is the signal that the
horizon is now long enough for the answer to mean "epidemic total".

## Interpretation and limitations

The result is an optimal start time **conditional on** a fixed 50% reduction,
a fixed ten-unit duration, a homogeneous closed population, perfect timing,
the 45-unit horizon, and the final-incidence objective. It is not a universal
recommendation. It is also a *local* minimizer that the grid scan supports
rather than a proven global one; with more decision variables that scan becomes
unaffordable and the distinction starts to matter. Because the horizon is finite,
part of any apparent gain can be infections deferred past $T$ rather than
averted, which is worth confirming by rerunning with a larger $T$ before quoting
a number.
Changing the cost of intervention, adding a peak-infection penalty, or
penalizing delayed action changes the problem. The rectangular callback also
creates an idealized instantaneous policy switch; a ramp-up, adherence model,
or stochastic transmission would be a different model. This chapter uses a
small bounded problem intentionally; continuous controls, path constraints,
and multistage uncertainty are deferred to the advanced optimal-control
appendix.

### Where to go next

- [Optimization.jl](https://docs.sciml.ai/Optimization/stable/) documents the
  solver choices and automatic-differentiation backends behind the four pieces
  above.
- [Frequentist parameter estimation](08-parameter-estimation.html) reuses this
  same `OptimizationProblem` pattern, with a likelihood as the objective instead
  of final incidence. This is the natural next step if you want to fit rather
  than choose.
- [Advanced optimal control](../appendices/08-advanced-optimal-control.html)
  replaces the single start time with a control *function* of time, using
  InfiniteOpt and SDDP.
- [Data-to-decision capstone](12-data-to-decision-capstone.html) runs the whole
  chain end to end: data, fit, and policy choice.

## Exercises

### Exercise 1 {#ch11-ex1}

Modify `run_scenario` to compare reductions of `0.25`, `0.50`, and `0.75`.
For each reduction, optimize the start time using the same bounds. Report
the start time and final incidence, and explain why the best timing need not
be the time at which infectious prevalence is largest.

### Exercise 2 {#ch11-ex2}

Make both the start time $t_1$ and the duration $d$ decision variables, and
define a new scalar objective

$$
J_\lambda(t_1,d)=C(T)+\lambda\int_0^{T}v(t)\,\mathrm dt
$$ {#eq-costed-objective}

for a nonnegative cost weight $\lambda$, over the admissible set

$$
0\leq t_1,\qquad 0\leq d\leq d_{\max},\qquad t_1+d\leq T,
$$ {#eq-costed-constraints}

so that the campaign both starts and finishes inside the decision horizon. For
the rectangular policy of @eq-rectangular-policy the integral evaluates to
$v_{\max}d$, so $\lambda$ is an exchange rate: it says how many infections one
unit of intervention time is worth. Explain which bound or constraint in
@eq-costed-constraints prevents the optimizer from selecting an unrealistically
long intervention, and what happens to the chosen $d$ when $\lambda=0$.
Implement the objective for at least two values of $\lambda$ and compare the
resulting policy choices — but choose them deliberately, so that they straddle
the weight at which the chosen duration changes. Two weights on the same side of
that threshold give different objective *values* while selecting an identical
policy, which is worth noticing rather than reporting as a comparison.
